2603-21809#s3: Retinal fundus imaging enables low-cost and scalable hypertension (HTN) screening, but HTN-related retinal cues are subtle, yielding high-variance predictions.
2603-21809#s4: Brain MRI provides stronger vascular and small-vessel-disease markers of HTN, yet it is expensive and rarely acquired alongside fundus images, resulting in modality-siloed datasets with disjoint MRI and fundus cohorts.
2603-21809#s5: We study this unpaired MRI - fundus regime and introduce Clinical Graph-Mediated Distillation (CGMD), a framework that transfers MRI-derived HTN knowledge to a fundus model without paired multimodal data.
2603-21809#s6: CGMD leverages shared structured biomarkers as a bridge by constructing a clinical similarity $k$NN graph spanning both cohorts.
2603-21809#s7: We train an MRI teacher, propagate its representations over the graph, and impute brain-informed representation targets for fundus patients.
2603-21809#s8: A fundus student is then trained with a joint objective combining HTN supervision, target distillation, and relational distillation.
2603-21809#s9: Experiments on our newly collected unpaired MRI - fundus - biomarker dataset show that CGMD consistently improves fundus-based HTN prediction over standard distillation and non-graph imputation baselines, with ablations confirming the importance of clinically grounded graph connectivity.
2603-21809#s12: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, underscoring the need for scalable methods to identify individuals at elevated vascular risk early~\cite{martin20242024}.
2603-21809#s13: Advances in computational imaging have enabled imaging-based risk phenotyping, where medical images are used to infer cardiometabolic and vascular risk factors at scale.
2603-21809#s14: High-fidelity modalities such as brain MRI can capture downstream injury patterns associated with chronic vascular risk and small-vessel disease~\cite{hainsworth2024cerebral,sole2024impact}.
2603-21809#s15: However, MRI is costly and unevenly available, limiting population-scale deployment, particularly in resource-constrained settings~\cite{murali2024bringing,hricak2025strengthening}.
2603-21809#s16: Retinal fundus imaging, by contrast, is inexpensive and widely deployable~\cite{nakayama2025comprehensive}, but it provides an indirect and incomplete readout of vascular pathology.
2603-21809#s17: HTN-related retinal cues are often subtle, heterogeneous, and confounded, leading to weak and high-variance signals that challenge robust inference~\cite{poplin2018prediction,zhang2020prediction,tan2022new}.
2603-21809#s18: A natural strategy is to transfer high-fidelity vascular signal from brain MRI to scalable retinal fundus imaging via cross-modal knowledge distillation, treating MRI as the teacher and fundus as the student.
2603-21809#s19: However, most cross-modal distillation and representation-alignment methods implicitly assume paired multimodal data - i.e., both modalities are acquired for the same individual - so that the teacher can provide a sample-specific target (logits or features) for each student image.
2603-21809#s20: In practice, paired MRI - fundus acquisitions are rarely available at scale: fundus imaging is routine and inexpensive, whereas MRI is resource-intensive and typically ordered under different clinical indications.
2603-21809#s21: Consequently, obtaining both modalities often requires dedicated multimodality sub-studies rather than standard care pipelines~\cite{sun2023protocol}.
2603-21809#s22: This yields a disjoint multi-cohort regime in which the teacher modality is systematically missing for the student cohort, rendering conventional paired distillation inapplicable and limiting approaches that depend on a small paired subset.
2603-21809#s23: These constraints motivate methods that can establish cross-cohort correspondence without co-acquisition, for example by leveraging shared structured clinical variables as a linking signal.
2603-21809#s24: Related work falls into three categories.
2603-21809#s25: First, paired cross-modal distillation~\cite{zhao2020knowledge} assumes paired acquisitions so a teacher on a superior modality can provide per-instance targets to supervise a student on a weaker modality.
2603-21809#s26: This assumption breaks when cohorts are disjoint and the superior modality is unavailable for the student cohort.
2603-21809#s27: Second, unpaired distillation~\cite{dou2020unpaired,jiang2021unpaired,yang2025umscs} uses modality-bridging translation or reconstruction to transfer supervision without one-to-one pairing, e.g., CMEDL~\cite{jiang2021unpaired} for unpaired MRI$\rightarrow$CT segmentation; these methods are largely tailored to closely related modalities of the same anatomy and do not address large modality gaps suc …
2603-21809#s28: Third, EHR-based patient similarity learning~\cite{gu2022structure} constructs clinical similarity graphs from structured variables, but has not been used to generate patient-specific distillation targets for cross-modal transfer across disjoint cohorts.
2603-21809#s29: To this end, we propose the Clinical Graph-Mediated Distillation (CGMD), a framework that transfers vascular representations from brain MRI to scalable retinal fundus imaging without paired acquisitions.
2603-21809#s30: To the best of our knowledge, CGMD is the first distillation approach that supports cross-modal transfer across disjoint cohorts and anatomically distinct modalities (e.g., brain MRI$\rightarrow$fundus) without subject-level correspondence.
2603-21809#s31: CGMD constructs a clinically grounded similarity graph from shared structured biomarkers, trains an MRI teacher on the MRI cohort, and propagates teacher embeddings over the graph to impute patient-specific distillation targets for fundus subjects in a separate cohort.
2603-21809#s32: A fundus student is then optimized with supervised HTN loss plus distillation to the imputed targets, enabling MRI-free deployment at inference.
2603-21809#s33: In summary, our main contributions are three-fold:
2603-21809#s34: We formalize an unpaired, disjoint-cohort MRI - fundus transfer setting, where paired distillation is infeasible and synthesis-based alignment is ill-posed due to the large anatomical modality gap.
2603-21809#s35: We propose Clinical Graph-Mediated Distillation (CGMD) framework that uses shared structured biomarkers to build a clinical similarity graph and propagate MRI teacher embeddings, producing patient-specific distillation targets for fundus training without paired acquisition.
2603-21809#s36: On a newly collected unpaired MRI - fundus - biomarker dataset, CGMD consistently improves fundus-based HTN prediction over standard distillation and non-graph imputation baselines; ablations verify that clinically grounded graph connectivity is critical for effective cross-cohort transfer.
2603-21809#s37: Fig.~\ref{fig1} overviews our cross-cohort graph-mediated distillation pipeline for transferring MRI-derived knowledge to fundus without paired subjects.
2603-21809#s38: Given disjoint cohorts, an MRI set $\mathcal{D}_B$ and a fundus set $\mathcal{D}_F$, we train an MRI teacher on $\mathcal{D}_B$ and extract patient embeddings.
2603-21809#s39: Using shared clinical biomarkers, we construct a $k$NN graph over MRI patients and smooth the embeddings to obtain denoised teacher priors (Sec.~\ref{sec:teacher_smoothing}).
2603-21809#s40: For each fundus patient in $\mathcal{D}_F$, we retrieve clinically nearest MRI patients and impute a patient-specific prior via weighted aggregation of the smoothed priors, using label-gating to encourage class-consistent transfer (Sec.~\ref{sec:prior_imputation}).
2603-21809#s41: We then train a fundus student with supervised loss, distillation to the imputed priors, and a relational term aligning fundus embedding similarities with those imputed priors (Sec.~\ref{sec:student_training}).
2603-21809#s42: At inference, only fundus inputs and routine biomarkers are required; no MRI is needed.

2603-21809#s154: These gains indicate that clinically grounded graph-based imputation provides more informative teacher targets than label-matched surrogate pairing, though the sensitivity trade-off should be weighed alongside the ranking-based gains.
2603-21809#s155: Prior distillation alone provides a solid baseline, while adding MRI-graph smoothing improves AUC with comparable AUPRC, supporting the hypothesis that smoothing denoises teacher embeddings before cross-cohort imputation.
2603-21809#s156: Fig.~\ref{fig:ablation_a} ablates data availability: performance improves as more informative inputs are provided, and CGMD remains best overall, indicating that MRI$\rightarrow$fundus adds benefit beyond clinical features and/or fundus images alone (or simple concatenation).
2603-21809#s157: Critically, the Fundus+Clinical condition already accesses the same 15 biomarkers used to build CGMD's targets, so the further gain to CGMD is attributable solely to the MRI-derived graph-mediated supervision, holding biomarker access fixed and ruling out a clinical-feature shortcut.
2603-21809#s158: Local baselines propagate teacher embeddings over a clinical similarity graph ($k$NN; GraphSAGE~\cite{hamilton2017inductive}) without label gating, while global baselines use class-conditional means (Global Class Mean) or cohort-level averages (Global Mean).
2603-21809#s159: CGMD outperforms all alternatives, consistent with the benefit of combining patient-specific, graph-mediated priors with class-consistent (label-gated) aggregation; however, as the local baselines also differ in propagation strategy, this comparison does not isolate label gating alone, and a controlled ablation is left to future work.
2603-21809#fig6: \begin{figure} \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{vis.png} \caption{Grad-CAM visualizations for a representative disagreement case.} \label{fig:gradcam} \end{figure}
2603-21809#s161: Fig.~\ref{fig:gradcam} shows a representative disagreement case in which CGMD predicts correctly while both baselines fail.
2603-21809#s162: The baselines concentrate on a narrow region near the optic disc, whereas CGMD attends to a broader retinal area, consistent with diffuse vascular feature utilization.
2603-21809#s163: We presented Clinical Graph-Mediated Distillation (CGMD), a resource-conscious framework for disjoint-cohort cross-modal transfer that uses shared biomarkers to propagate MRI teacher embeddings as patient-specific distillation targets for fundus training requiring neither paired acquisitions nor MRI at deployment.
2603-21809#s164: On 5-fold cross-validation, CGMD outperformed adapted distillation baselines, with ablations confirming the importance of clinically grounded graph structure.
2603-21809#s165: As a single-center study with a modest fundus cohort ($n{=}112$), these results are preliminary; future work will pursue external validation on larger multi-center cohorts, extending to other disjoint-cohort modality pairs.
